blocks.text: His face was strong—very strong. His nose was curved like an eagle's beak. It was thin, with a high bridge, and the nostrils were curved in a strange way. His forehead was high and rounded like a dome. His hair grew thinly around the temples, but it was thick everywhere else. His eyebrows were very heavy and almost met over his nose. The hair in them was so thick that it seemed to curl because there was so much of it. He had a heavy moustache. Under it, as far as I could see, his mouth was fixed and looked rather cruel. His teeth were white and strangely sharp. They stuck out over his lips. His lips were remarkably red, and this showed amazing life and energy in a man of his age. As for the rest, his ears were pale, and they were extremely pointed at the tops. His chin was broad and strong. His cheeks were firm, though thin. Overall, he looked extraordinarily pale.

Until then, I had only noticed the backs of his hands. They had been lying on his knees in the firelight, and they had seemed rather white and fine. But now I saw them close to me, and I could not help noticing that they were rather rough. They were broad, with short, thick fingers. Strangely, there were hairs in the centre of the palm. The nails were long and fine, and they were cut to a sharp point. The Count leaned over me, and his hands touched me. I could not stop myself from shivering. Perhaps his breath smelled bad, but a horrible feeling of sickness came over me. Whatever I did, I could not hide it. The Count clearly noticed it, and he drew back. He gave a grim sort of smile, which showed his sticking-out teeth more than he had shown them so far. Then he sat down again on his own side of the fireplace. We were both silent for a while. As I looked towards the window, I saw the first faint line of light from the coming dawn. Everything seemed strangely still. But as I listened, I heard what sounded like many wolves howling, down below in the valley. The Count's eyes shone, and he said:—
“Listen to them—the children of the night. What music they make!” I suppose he saw some expression on my face that seemed strange to him, because he added:—
“Ah, sir, you people who live in cities cannot understand the feelings of the hunter.” Then he stood up and said:—

“But you must be tired. Your bedroom is all ready, and tomorrow you may sleep as late as you like. I have to be away until the afternoon, so sleep well and dream well!” He bowed politely, and he opened the door to the eight-sided room for me himself. Then I went into my bedroom....
I am lost in a sea of wonders. I doubt; I fear; I think strange things that I dare not admit even to my own soul. May God keep me safe, if only for the sake of the people I love!

7 May.—It is early morning again, but I have rested and enjoyed the last twenty-four hours. I slept until late in the day, and I woke up by myself. When I had dressed, I went into the room where we had eaten supper. There I found a cold breakfast on the table. There was coffee too, and it was kept hot because the pot stood on the hearth by the fire. There was a card on the table, and on it was written:—

“I have to be away for a while. Do not wait for me.—D.” I started eating and enjoyed a big meal. When I had finished, I looked for a bell to let the servants know that I was done. But I could not find one. There are certainly some strange things missing in this house, especially when I see such extraordinary signs of wealth all around me. The plates, dishes and other things on the table are made of gold. They are so beautifully made that they must be worth an enormous amount. Then there are the curtains, the covers of the chairs and sofas, and the hangings around my bed. They are made of the most expensive and beautiful cloth. They must have been worth a fortune when they were made, because they are centuries old. Yet they are in excellent condition. I saw something like them at Hampton Court, but there they were worn, torn at the edges and eaten by moths. But still, there is no mirror in any of the rooms. There is not even a small mirror for dressing on my table. I had to get my little shaving mirror from my bag before I could shave or brush my hair. I have not yet seen a servant anywhere. I have not heard any sound near the castle except the howling of wolves. Some time after I had finished my meal, I looked around for something to read. I do not know whether to call that meal breakfast or dinner, because I had it between five and six o'clock. I wanted something to read because I did not like to walk around the castle until I had asked the Count's permission. There was absolutely nothing in the room—no book, no newspaper, not even anything to write with. So I opened another door in the room and found a sort of library. I tried the door opposite mine, but it was locked.
